records.sourceFile: Effect of a 90-Minute Nap at Different Times of the Day on Physical Performance, Psycho-Cognitive Responses, and Perceived Recovery in Trained Youth Male Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Jebabli A, Delleli S, Mahdi N, Ben Maaoui K, Del Coso J, Chtourou H, Ardigò LP, Ouergui I. Effect of a 90-Minute Nap at Different Times of the Day on Physical Performance, Psycho-Cognitive Responses, and Perceived Recovery in Trained Youth Male Athletes. Sports. 2025;13:395.
paper.abstract: This randomized crossover study tested whether the timing of a 90-minute nap changes afternoon physical performance, psycho-cognitive responses, and perceived recovery in trained youth male athletes.
paper.tldr: In 14 trained young men, a 90-minute nap beginning at 13:00 improved selected shuttle-run and attention outcomes compared with later or no-nap conditions. Effects were not consistent across fatigue, feeling, sleep, and recovery measures, so the study supports a promising timing option rather than a universal nap prescription.
paper.methods: Fourteen trained male athletes aged 18 plus or minus 1 year completed four randomized crossover conditions: no nap with testing at 13:00 or 15:00 and a 90-minute nap beginning at 13:00 or 15:00. Outcomes included repeated 5-m shuttle-run best and total distance, fatigue index, RPE, soreness, perceived recovery, digit cancelation, feeling, sleepiness, sleep quality, and Hooper questionnaire scores.
paper.findings: Total shuttle-run distance was higher after the 13:00 nap than after the 15:00 nap and 15:00 no-nap condition. Best distance was higher after the 13:00 nap than after either no-nap condition, and digit-cancelation performance also improved. RPE was higher in the 13:00 nap condition, while fatigue index, feeling state, and Hooper scores did not differ significantly.
paper.limitations: The study used a small sample of trained young men, one nap duration, and one intermittent running protocol. It did not personalize timing by chronotype or sleep need, and standardized post-nap light and television exposure may have influenced responses.
paper.practicalImplications: When schedules permit and prior sleep is controlled, trialing an early-afternoon 90-minute nap may help selected athletes preparing for later training or competition. Evaluate the athlete's sleep inertia, logistics, and repeated individual response before routine use.
paper.athleteDev: Teach sleep planning as an individualized performance skill. Track bedtime, wake time, nap timing, post-nap alertness, and training response so athletes learn whether napping supports their schedule rather than treating it as mandatory.
paper.rtp: A nap may support perceived readiness during return-to-training days, but it does not replace medical clearance, progressive exposure, or objective task tolerance. Avoid interpreting temporary alertness as restored tissue or systemic capacity.

records.sourceFile: Relationship between training load and recovery in collegiate American football players during pre-season training.pdf

paper.citation: Jagim AR, Wright GA, Camic CL, Kisiolek JN, Luedke J, Oliver JM, Fischer KM, Jones MT. Relationship between training load and recovery in collegiate American football players during pre-season training. Science and Medicine in Football. 2021;5(4):330-338.
paper.abstract: This 14-day collegiate American football cohort study examined how internal and external practice-load measures related to next-day neuromuscular performance and perceived recovery during preseason.
paper.tldr: Session RPE load and mechanical load related to different next-day recovery signals in 17 collegiate football players. The study supports a low-cost multimethod monitoring approach, but its small one-team sample does not justify universal thresholds or single-score readiness decisions.
paper.methods: Seventeen players, including six linemen and 11 non-linemen, wore accelerometer and heart-rate sensors during preseason practice and reported session RPE immediately afterward. Before the next practice they completed a drop-jump reactive strength index test and rated perceived recovery; loaded countermovement-jump performance was assessed before and after preseason.
paper.findings: Each unit increase in session-RPE load was associated with a 0.03-unit decline in next-day reactive strength index, while each unit increase in mechanical load was associated with a 0.01-unit reduction in perceived recovery. Non-linemen accumulated greater mechanical load, and load and recovery variables were generally lower in week 2 than week 1.
paper.limitations: Only 17 athletes from one team completed analysis after seven monitored players were excluded because of injury. Position subgroups were very small, observation lasted 14 days, and the relationships may change across season phases, programs, or monitoring systems.
paper.practicalImplications: Pair a simple internal-load measure such as session RPE with an external mechanical-load measure and at least one next-day recovery check. Review trends by athlete and position rather than collapsing all players into one team threshold.
paper.athleteDev: Use monitoring conversations to help players connect perceived intensity, contact and movement exposure, sleep, soreness, and next-day output. The goal is better self-regulation and communication, not punishment for reporting fatigue.
paper.rtp: Returning players may need individualized comparison with their own recent workload and recovery pattern. A normal subjective score or jump result alone should not override clinical status, exposure progression, or sport-specific function.

records.sourceFile: Decreased isometric neck strength is a risk factor for head  neck and face injuries in professional rugby league players.pdf

paper.citation: Hides JA, Brown DA, Anning LN, Blanch PD, Leung FT. Decreased isometric neck strength is a risk factor for head, neck and face injuries in professional rugby league players. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024. Published online ahead of print.
paper.abstract: This exploratory prospective study tested whether preseason cervical strength, endurance, and proprioception measures were associated with head, neck, and face injuries causing missed games in professional rugby league players.
paper.tldr: In one 32-player professional rugby league squad, lower neck-extensor strength and lateral-flexor asymmetry were associated with greater odds of head, neck, or face injury. The findings justify further testing and targeted assessment, not universal cut points or a claim that neck strengthening prevents injury.
paper.methods: Thirty-two adult male players from one professional Queensland rugby league squad completed preseason measures of cervical flexor, extensor, and lateral-flexor isometric strength, flexor endurance, and joint-position error. Preseason and playing-season injuries leading to missed games were recorded, and unadjusted odds ratios were estimated from cross-tabulations.
paper.findings: Players below the study's extensor-strength cut points of 36.4 kg or 3.4 N/kg had an unadjusted injury odds ratio of 8.0, and those with a left-to-right lateral-flexor strength ratio below 0.91 had an odds ratio of 12.6. Confidence intervals were wide and the asymmetry association was a novel finding.
paper.limitations: This was a convenience sample from one team with few injuries, wide confidence intervals, and insufficient power for some variables. Analyses were unadjusted, multiple comparisons were not corrected, and exposure, collision frequency, position, and prior-injury confounding were not fully modeled.
paper.practicalImplications: Cervical strength and side-to-side capacity can be included in contact-sport profiling when staff can test reliably and connect findings to progressive training. Treat the published cut points as local exploratory references and validate changes against the athlete's own function and exposure.
paper.athleteDev: Build neck capacity progressively alongside tackle technique, trunk control, and contact preparation. Explain that strength is one modifiable factor within a broader injury-risk system rather than a guarantee of protection.
paper.rtp: After head, neck, or face injury, cervical testing may complement symptom, neurological, range-of-motion, strength-endurance, and contact-tolerance criteria. Do not use these preseason cut points as stand-alone clearance tests.

records.sourceFile: Effect of training day match and length of the microcycle on the worst-case scenarios in professional soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Oliva-Lozano JM, Gómez-Carmona CD, Rojas-Valverde D, Fortes V, Pino-Ortega J. Effect of training day, match, and length of the microcycle on the worst-case scenarios in professional soccer players. Research in Sports Medicine. 2021. Published online ahead of print.
paper.abstract: This professional soccer cohort study described rolling worst-case locomotor demands across training days and matches and examined whether training-day peaks differed with microcycle length.
paper.tldr: Across 23 professional soccer players, 43 training sessions, and 13 matches, match peak demands exceeded training across all tested durations. Training peaks varied by day and microcycle length, supporting locally calibrated rolling peak-demand planning rather than fixed generic drill targets.
paper.methods: Twenty-three Spanish second-division outfield players were monitored across four competitive mesocycles comprising 43 training sessions and 13 matches. Rolling 1-, 3-, 5-, and 10-minute worst-case windows were calculated for total distance, high-speed-running distance, and sprinting distance and compared by day relative to match and microcycle length.
paper.findings: Matches produced the highest worst-case values at every intensity and duration. Among training days, the largest distance, high-speed, and sprint peaks generally occurred four or three days before the match and one day after; training-day peaks differed across shorter, regular, and longer microcycles, while match peaks did not.
paper.limitations: Data came from one team and four mesocycles, excluded goalkeepers and incomplete sessions, and depended on GPS accuracy. The observational analysis did not determine whether reproducing match peaks in training improves adaptation, performance, or injury outcomes.
paper.practicalImplications: Calculate rolling peak demands from the team's own match data, then design selected drills and weekly exposures around relevant time windows. Adjust targets by position, schedule length, recent match minutes, and the intended purpose of each day.
paper.athleteDev: Expose athletes progressively to the intensity and duration combinations their roles require while preserving technical quality. Use peak-demand data to explain preparation goals and avoid turning a single maximal value into the target for every session.
paper.rtp: Compare a returning player's rolling high-intensity exposures with role-specific training and match references as one part of reconditioning. Peak running exposure does not replace clinical criteria, movement quality, contact readiness, or accumulated-load tolerance.

records.sourceFile: Effects of an 8-week pre-season targeted training on sprinting performance, agility and lower limb muscular asymmetries in elite soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Gołaś A, Pietraszewski P, Roczniok R, Terbalyan A, Maszczyk A, Opaliński R, Zając A. Effects of an 8-week pre-season targeted training on sprinting performance, agility and lower limb muscular asymmetries in elite soccer players. Biology of Sport. 2024;41(4):69-76.
paper.abstract: This randomized preseason study tested whether adding a targeted unilateral movement-pattern program improved sprinting, change-of-direction performance, and lower-limb muscle-activation asymmetry in elite soccer players.
paper.tldr: An eight-week bundled program of unilateral bodyweight exercises performed four days per week improved selected sprint and change-of-direction outcomes in 32 elite soccer players. The study does not show which component mattered or that changing EMG asymmetry prevents injury.
paper.methods: Thirty-two elite soccer players were randomized to 16-player control and experimental groups. Both were tested before and after an eight-week preseason for 5- and 30-m sprint, randomized ZigZag change of direction, and bilateral quadriceps, hamstring, and gluteal EMG; the experimental group added six unilateral bodyweight exercises four times weekly with progressive volume.
paper.findings: The experimental program produced statistically significant improvement in 5-m and 30-m sprint performance and change of direction, with the largest gains in the change-of-direction test and a reduced change-of-direction deficit. The authors also reported altered activation patterns and partial reductions in muscular asymmetry.
paper.limitations: The small sample, single preseason, and bundled intervention limit attribution to any one exercise. Surface EMG measured activation rather than muscle force or adaptation, and no prospective injury outcome was collected despite proposed injury-risk implications.
paper.practicalImplications: A short, frequent unilateral movement-pattern circuit may be one component of preseason preparation when it complements sprint, change-of-direction, and resistance work. Track performance and tolerance directly instead of assuming EMG normalization is the mechanism.
paper.athleteDev: Progress movement quality, unilateral control, acceleration, and change-of-direction skill together. Individualize volume and exercise difficulty so added accessory work supports rather than displaces high-value field and strength exposures.
paper.rtp: The circuit may provide low-equipment supplemental work during late reconditioning, but return decisions require progressive high-speed running, braking, cutting, and sport-specific exposure rather than asymmetry or EMG results alone.

records.sourceFile: Return to play performance and career duration after ACL rupture - A case control study in the five biggest football nations in Europe.pdf

paper.citation: Niederer D, Engeroff T, Wilke J, Vogt L, Banzer W. Return to play, performance, and career duration after anterior cruciate ligament rupture: A case-control study in the five biggest football nations in Europe. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2018.
paper.abstract: This five-year media-based case-control study compared return, competitive level, match performance, and career survival after ACL rupture with matched controls in elite male European soccer.
paper.tldr: Nearly all 125 injured professional players returned after ACL rupture, but only 59.4% returned at the same level and career survival and match performance were lower than in matched controls. Binary return rate therefore overstates recovery of competitive function.
paper.methods: The authors identified 132 ACL ruptures in 125 male players from the first two leagues of England, Spain, Italy, Germany, and France during 2010/11 and 2011/12. Each injured player was matched to two controls by age, position, country and league, and market value; validated public databases supplied five-year participation, injury, performance, and career data.
paper.findings: The overall return-to-play rate was 98.2%, but return at the same level was 59.4%. Five years after return, 69.9% remained in football and 40.9% at the same level; career duration differed from controls, and scoring points, passing measures, and minutes played were lower in the return and post-return seasons.
paper.limitations: Media sources did not provide clinical confirmation, injury side, surgical technique, rehabilitation detail, symptoms, or non-time-loss history. Although database validation and matching strengthen the design, residual confounding and incomplete injury characterization remain.
paper.practicalImplications: Report return as a multidimensional outcome: availability, same-level participation, minutes, role, performance, subsequent injury, and career continuity. Prepare stakeholders for a high chance of playing again without promising immediate or complete competitive restoration.
paper.athleteDev: Maintain long-horizon physical, technical, and psychological development after the first match back. Continued exposure progression and role support matter because the return date is the start of performance restoration, not its endpoint.
paper.rtp: Clearance should distinguish return to training, return to competition, return to the prior level, and sustainable performance. Monitor match minutes, high-intensity actions, confidence, knee response, and subsequent injuries beyond initial return.

records.sourceFile: Reconsidering Exercise Selection with EMG - Poor Agreement between Ranking Hip Exercises with Gluteal EMG and Muscle Force.pdf

paper.citation: Collings TJ, Bourne MN, Barrett RS, Meinders E, Gonçalves B, Shield A, Diamond LE. Reconsidering Exercise Selection with EMG: Poor Agreement between Ranking Hip Exercises with Gluteal EMG and Muscle Force. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2025. Published ahead of print.
paper.abstract: This laboratory study compared rankings of hip-focused exercises based on gluteal surface EMG with rankings based on muscle-force estimates from neuromusculoskeletal modeling.
paper.tldr: Eight hip exercises ranked differently when judged by peak gluteal EMG versus estimated gluteal muscle force in 14 female footballers. EMG may help with within-person comparisons of similar tasks, but peak activation alone is a weak basis for choosing among biomechanically different exercises.
paper.methods: Fourteen healthy female footballers aged 18-30 performed eight hip-focused exercises using body weight and 12-repetition-maximum loads. Full-body kinematics, ground-reaction forces, and EMG from 12 lower-limb muscles were inputs to a neuromusculoskeletal model; normalized exercise rankings and EMG-force relationships were compared.
paper.findings: Rank correlations between EMG and estimated force were weak, with Spearman rho values of 0.29-0.51. Peak EMG alone explained 5% of gluteus-maximus and 19% of gluteus-medius peak-force variation across exercises, although models accounting for participant and exercise effects explained 80-85% within that structured context.
paper.limitations: The sample was small and female, only eight exercises were studied, and force estimates were not directly validated against in-vivo muscle force. Muscle-tendon parameters were not fully personalized, and neither proxy measured chronic adaptation or clinical outcome.
paper.practicalImplications: Choose exercises from the athlete's goal, joint mechanics, external load, range, tolerance, and progression options. Use EMG to answer narrow within-athlete questions among comparable tasks, not to create universal best-exercise rankings.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes that feeling or seeing high activation does not automatically mean greater force or better adaptation. Progress exercise challenge through load, range, intent, control, and transfer to the required task.
paper.rtp: During rehabilitation, do not advance or reject an exercise from EMG amplitude alone. Combine symptoms, movement quality, strength capacity, loading tolerance, and task-specific progression with any instrumented information.

records.sourceFile: The Application of Blood Flow        Restriction- Lessons From the Laboratory.pdf

paper.citation: Mattocks KT, Jessee MB, Mouser JG, Dankel SJ, Buckner SL, Bell ZW, Owens JG, Abe T, Loenneke JP. The Application of Blood Flow Restriction: Lessons From the Laboratory. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2018;17(4):129-134.
paper.abstract: This narrative review translated laboratory evidence on blood-flow restriction into practical guidance for exercise and rehabilitation, emphasizing how cuff and individual characteristics determine the applied restriction.
paper.tldr: Blood-flow restriction can produce muscular adaptation with low loads and may help when heavy loading is not appropriate, but pressure is not interchangeable across cuffs or athletes. Individualized arterial-occlusion-based dosing and trained oversight are central safety requirements.
paper.methods: The authors narratively reviewed laboratory and clinical evidence on blood-flow restriction alone and with low-load resistance or aerobic exercise. They discussed cuff width and material, limb size, arterial occlusion, common repetition structures, practical wrapping, rehabilitation applications, and safety considerations.
paper.findings: Low-load blood-flow-restriction training can increase muscle size and strength and may support rehabilitation or disuse periods. Wider cuffs require less absolute pressure, larger limbs generally require more pressure, and the same absolute pressure can create very different restriction across individuals; the review recommends relative individualized pressure.
paper.limitations: This was not a systematic review or a new comparative trial. Protocols and populations varied, adverse-event evidence was incomplete, and practical elastic wrapping had limited validation outside young resistance-trained men and uncertain vascular effects.
paper.practicalImplications: Use blood-flow restriction only within an established clinical or performance protocol that includes contraindication screening, appropriate equipment, individualized pressure, staff competency, symptom monitoring, and documented progression.
paper.athleteDev: Position blood-flow restriction as a temporary loading tool rather than a shortcut. Preserve technical development and progressively restore conventional strength, power, and sport exposure as capacity permits.
paper.rtp: Blood-flow restriction may help maintain or rebuild muscle when high external loads are temporarily limited. It does not establish tissue readiness or sport clearance and should remain subordinate to diagnosis-specific healing, strength, function, and exposure criteria.

records.sourceFile: The effect of the Copenhagen Adduction and Nordic Hamstring exercises on muscle strength and athletic performance - A quasi-experimental study.pdf

paper.citation: Pippas C, Dagloukiaris N, Antypas A, Touloupis E, Gioftsos G. The effect of the Copenhagen Adduction and Nordic Hamstring exercises on muscle strength and athletic performance: a quasi-experimental study. Journal of Orthopaedic Reports. 2024;100524.
paper.abstract: This quasi-experimental preseason study examined strength and performance changes after adolescent male soccer players combined Nordic hamstring and Copenhagen adduction exercises for four weeks.
paper.tldr: The twice-weekly four-week program increased hamstring and hip-adduction strength in 38 adolescent male soccer players, but did not produce clear jump or sprint improvement. The uncontrolled design cannot separate the program from normal preseason change.
paper.methods: Thirty-eight male players from one Greek soccer club completed a progressive four-week preseason program combining Nordic hamstring and Copenhagen adduction exercises twice weekly. Hand-held dynamometry assessed isometric hamstring and eccentric adduction strength; jump, sprint, and perceived-exertion outcomes were also recorded.
paper.findings: Isometric hamstring strength increased about 11% and eccentric hip-adduction strength about 17%. Jump performance declined 5-7%, sprint performance changed about 2-3% with inconsistent statistical significance, and perceived exertion did not differ meaningfully between the exercises.
paper.limitations: The study lacked randomization and a control group, experienced substantial loss to follow-up because testing occurred on separate occasions, and ran alongside normal preseason training. These limitations weaken causal attribution and may contribute to imprecise performance findings.
paper.practicalImplications: Nordic hamstring and Copenhagen adduction exercises can be paired as a concise targeted-strength block, but staff should manage preseason dose and evaluate sprint and jump response separately rather than assuming automatic performance transfer.
paper.athleteDev: Build eccentric hamstring and hip-adduction capacity progressively with sound technique and tolerable soreness. Integrate the work with sprinting, jumping, and soccer practice so targeted strength supports broader development.
paper.rtp: These exercises may contribute to criterion-based hamstring or groin rehabilitation after appropriate progression. Strength improvement alone does not establish sprinting, cutting, kicking, or competition readiness.

records.sourceFile: Acute and post-acute COVID-19 presentations in athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Lemes IR, Smaira FI, Ribeiro WJD, Favero NK, Matos LDNJ, Pinto ALS, Dolan E, Gualano B, Coalition SPORT-COVID-19. Acute and post-acute COVID-19 presentations in athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis characterized acute symptoms, persistent symptoms, and cardiac findings after COVID-19 in professional, amateur, collegiate, and university athletes.
paper.tldr: Across 43 studies and 11,518 athletes, most infections were mild or asymptomatic and severe illness was uncommon, while a minority reported persistent symptoms. Cardiac abnormalities varied with testing and controlled studies did not confirm that COVID-19 caused myocardial involvement.
paper.methods: MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus, and SPORTDiscus were searched for observational athlete studies published from 2019 through January 6, 2022. Forty-three studies with 11,518 athletes met criteria; Joanna Briggs Institute tools assessed risk of bias and random-effects models pooled acute, post-acute, and cardiac event rates.
paper.findings: The pooled asymptomatic estimate was 25.5% and severe acute disease 1.3%, indicating about 94% experienced mild or no acute symptoms. Persistent symptoms were estimated at 8.3%. Myocardial involvement was 5.0% among athletes receiving any cardiac testing and 2.5% with MRI, but controlled studies did not establish causality.
paper.limitations: Studies varied substantially in athlete selection, testing indication, timing, symptom and cardiac definitions, follow-up, and risk of bias. Serial assessments were uncommon, confidence intervals were wide for persistent symptoms, and imaging findings were not consistently linked with symptoms or clinical consequences.
paper.practicalImplications: Most athletes can follow a symptom-guided graded return after appropriate medical review, but persistent cardiopulmonary, systemic, or exercise-intolerance symptoms warrant individualized assessment. Avoid indiscriminate imaging or reassurance based solely on population averages.
paper.athleteDev: Support honest symptom reporting and a gradual rebuild of aerobic, strength, and sport-specific work after illness. Normalize short-term modification so athletes do not hide symptoms to accelerate return.
paper.rtp: Return timing should reflect illness severity, current symptoms, exercise response, and relevant medical findings. Persistent chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, or disproportionate fatigue requires clinical evaluation; incidental imaging findings need expert interpretation.

records.sourceFile: Acute effects of cluster and rest redistribution set structures on mechanical, metabolic, and perceptual fatigue during and after resistance training - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Jukic I, García-Ramos A, Helms ER, McGuigan MR, Tufano JJ. Acute Effects of Cluster and Rest Redistribution Set Structures on Mechanical, Metabolic, and Perceptual Fatigue During and After Resistance Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis compared traditional resistance-training sets with cluster and rest-redistribution structures for acute mechanical, metabolic, and perceptual responses.
paper.tldr: Across 32 studies, distributing rest within or between sets generally preserved velocity and power and reduced lactate and perceived exertion. Cluster sets often showed larger effects partly because they added more total rest, and the review did not establish superior long-term adaptation.
paper.methods: Five databases were searched through June 2019 under PRISMA guidance for healthy-adult studies comparing traditional, cluster, or rest-redistribution sets. Thirty-two studies were included, with random-effects meta-analysis, subgroup analysis, and meta-regression used where data allowed.
paper.findings: Alternative structures improved absolute mean and peak velocity and power and more strongly reduced the decline in velocity and power during and after training. They also reduced lactate accumulation and perceived exertion; cluster sets generally produced larger fatigue-mitigation effects than rest redistribution.
paper.limitations: Exercises, loads, repetitions, failure proximity, total rest, training status, and outcomes varied. Cluster protocols often increased total rest relative to traditional sets, subgroup samples were small, and the evidence primarily concerned acute responses rather than chronic strength, hypertrophy, or power development.
paper.practicalImplications: Use clusters or redistributed rest when the session priority is preserving repetition speed, power, or technical quality or constraining acute fatigue. Match total rest when evaluating whether the set structure itself adds value, and preserve traditional sets when metabolic stress is intentional.
paper.athleteDev: Teach athletes to align set structure with the day's objective. Repeated high-quality efforts may benefit from planned micro-rest, while work-capacity or hypertrophy goals may deliberately accept more fatigue.
paper.rtp: Alternative set structures can help reintroduce resistance work while limiting velocity loss and perceived strain. They do not replace diagnosis-specific load limits, symptom response, or progression to continuous sets and sport demands.

records.sourceFile: Acute effects of overspeed stimuli with towing system on athletic sprint performance - A systematic review with meta-analysis.pdf

paper.citation: Cecilia-Gallego P, Odriozola A, Beltran-Garrido JV, Álvarez-Herms J. Acute effects of overspeed stimuli with towing system on athletic sprint performance: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2022.
paper.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated acute sprint-speed, spatiotemporal, force, and electromyographic responses when athletes sprinted with towing-assisted overspeed systems.
paper.tldr: Towing assistance acutely increased maximum running speed and stride length and reduced contact time across 16 studies. The evidence could not determine whether these changes reflected athlete neuromuscular behavior or direct device assistance, and it did not establish retained unassisted speed gains.
paper.methods: PubMed, SPORTDiscus, and Google Scholar were searched using PRISMA methods. Sixteen studies involving 240 men and 56 women aged 14-31 years were included, and acute assisted-sprint outcomes were pooled where appropriate.
paper.findings: Overspeed towing produced a large acute increase in maximum running speed, a moderate increase in stride length, a small increase in flight time, a trivial increase in stride rate, and a small decrease in contact time. Ground-reaction-force and EMG evidence was too inconsistent to explain the mechanism.
paper.limitations: Towing systems, assistance loads, sprint protocols, athlete levels, and biomechanical measures varied, with limited elite-sprinter evidence. Most outcomes were immediate responses under assistance, force and EMG data were sparse, and long-term unassisted transfer was not established.
paper.practicalImplications: If overspeed towing is used, quantify and individualize assistance, preserve upright mechanics, and stop when athletes lose control. Evaluate subsequent unassisted sprint performance over time rather than counting the assisted speed itself as adaptation.
paper.athleteDev: Introduce supramaximal exposure only after athletes demonstrate robust unassisted sprint mechanics and adequate tissue capacity. Keep assisted work as a small, monitored complement to acceleration, maximum-velocity, strength, and technical training.
paper.rtp: Overspeed towing is generally a late-stage performance tool, not an early return intervention. Require symptom-free high-speed running and progressive unassisted exposure before considering assisted velocities.
